title: Training and Development Specialists
description: Design or conduct work-related training and development programs to improve individual skills or organizational performance. May analyze organizational training needs or evaluate training effectiveness.
tasks: Present information with a variety of instructional techniques or formats, such as role playing, simulations, team exercises, group discussions, videos, or lectures.
Obtain, organize, or develop training procedure manuals, guides, or course materials, such as handouts or visual materials.
Evaluate modes of training delivery, such as in-person or virtual, to optimize training effectiveness, training costs, or environmental impacts.
Offer specific training programs to help workers maintain or improve job skills.
Assess training needs through surveys, interviews with employees, focus groups, or consultation with managers, instructors, or customer representatives.
Monitor, evaluate, or record training activities or program effectiveness.
Design, plan, organize, or direct orientation and training programs for employees or customers.
Develop alternative training methods if expected improvements are not seen.
Evaluate training materials prepared by instructors, such as outlines, text, or handouts.
Monitor training costs and prepare budget reports to justify expenditures.
Devise programs to develop executive potential among employees in lower-level positions.
Keep up with developments in area of expertise by reading current journals, books, or magazine articles.
Attend meetings or seminars to obtain information for use in training programs or to inform management of training program status.
Coordinate recruitment and placement of training program participants.
Select and assign instructors to conduct training.
Negotiate contracts with clients for desired training outcomes, fees, or expenses.
Supervise, evaluate, or refer instructors to skill development classes.
Schedule classes based on availability of classrooms, equipment, or instructors.
Refer trainees to employer relations representatives, to locations offering job placement assistance, or to appropriate social services agencies, if warranted.
Develop or implement training programs related to efficiency, recycling, or other issues with environmental impacts.

role_contexts.Face-to-Face Discussions with Individual: Once a week or more but not every day
role_contexts.Indoors, Environmentally Controlled: Once a week or more but not every day

psychological_profile.core_drive: The need to witness measurable transformation in others—to see the moment when someone who couldn't suddenly can, and to know they were the catalyst.
psychological_profile.decision_style: Under pressure, they default to rapid prototyping: build a small version, test it live, iterate in real-time rather than wait for perfect information. They distrust decisions made in conference rooms without immediate participant feedback.
psychological_profile.attention_pattern: They instantly scan for engagement signals—who's leaning forward, who's checking their phone, who's asking clarifying questions—and treat disengagement as the only meaningful failure metric. They overlook structural inefficiencies if the room feels alive.
psychological_profile.conflict_stance: Their first impulse is to reframe disagreement as a 'learning opportunity' for both parties, which often infuriates direct antagonists who wanted a fight. Conflict carries the specific cost of feeling like a personal teaching failure.
psychological_profile.risk_orientation: They accept high interpersonal risk (public failure, awkward silence, challenged credibility) but resist systemic risk (organization-wide rollout without pilot data, irreversible policy changes).
psychological_profile.social_posture: They default to 'the person running the room without owning it'—orchestrating energy and participation while deflecting formal leadership recognition. They seek connection through shared experience rather than sustained intimacy.
psychological_profile.relationship_to_authority: They treat hierarchy as raw material to be worked with—neither obeyed nor resisted, but strategically engaged to secure resources and protect participants from organizational interference.
psychological_profile.failure_response: First reaction is shame disguised as professional concern ('the material wasn't engaging enough'). Second response is rapid, almost compulsive redesign—often abandoning sound elements that merely had bad timing.
psychological_profile.cognitive_bias: They systematically overestimate how much of their own energy and charisma can be transferred to others, believing that presence and preparation can overcome structural barriers like time, compensation, or genuine lack of interest.
psychological_profile.inner_contradiction: They need to be seen as essential to transformation yet resent dependency—wanting credit for ignition while insisting learners 'did it themselves.'
psychological_profile.non_negotiable: They will not deliver content they haven't personally tested with real humans, no matter how approved, researched, or demanded by leadership.
psychological_profile.recurring_resentment: People who treat training as a checkbox or punishment—managers who send 'problem employees' to be 'fixed,' or organizations that schedule development during lunch without eating.
psychological_profile.rejected_premise: They quietly reject 'efficiency' as a training virtue, viewing compressed timelines and cost-cutting as direct attacks on the conditions required for actual change.
psychological_profile.instinctive_blame_target: When programs fail, they first blame the organizational conditions—scheduling, manager support, participant selection—before considering that their design or delivery might be the actual problem.
